interrogator_dossier:
# Sprinklr, Inc. (CXM) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $6.07 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars, intraday Monday 2026-07-27; up 6.9% from Friday's $5.685 close). Market value about $1.50 billion. The stock has traded between $4.72 and $9.40 over the past year, is down about 22% so far in 2026 and down about 35% over twelve months, but is up roughly 18% in the past month.

**Transcripts reviewed:** six consecutive quarterly calls — 2025-03-12 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2025), 2025-06-04, 2025-09-03, 2025-12-03, 2026-03-11 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2026) and 2026-06-03 (first quarter of fiscal 2027, retrieved live because it was missing from the supplied file). Sprinklr's fiscal year ends 31 January, so "fiscal 2027" is the year running to 31 January 2027.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

This is a single, unbroken chief-executive narrative — and that is both its strength and the thing to be most careful about.

Rory Read took over as chief executive in late 2024 and, from his first call (March 2025), told investors exactly one story: a three-phase turnaround. Phase one is business optimisation (cut costs, redraw the sales territories, install a management reporting system). Phase two is transition and execution (embed the changes, fix the customer relationships). Phase three is acceleration (grow again). He has never deviated from that frame, he has never contradicted it, and he repeats the same vocabulary — "ambidextrous strategy", "business management system", "Project Bear Hug", "technical debt", "a work in progress" — in every call. Consistency of story is genuinely rare and it counts in his favour.

What has changed is the **clock**. In March 2025 the plan was: transition through fiscal 2026, "see the business begin to bend" during that year. By June 2025 he was saying "you look for a bend as we go through the second half into FY 2027". By March 2026 the acceleration phase had moved to fiscal 2028, and Patrick Walravens of Citizens JMP said so out loud: "previously, we thought the acceleration phase would happen in the second half of fiscal '27 and now we're talking about fiscal '28. Is that fair?" Read's answer did not deny it — he re-described the original ranges as "12 to 18 months" and added, "we could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way." By June 2026 the destination is unchanged and still one year out. **The story has not changed; the finish line has moved roughly twelve months in eighteen months of elapsed time.**

The content of the story has also shifted in one important way. In 2025 the growth driver was operational: fix renewals, fix implementations, sell to the Global 2000. By the March 2026 and June 2026 calls the growth driver is artificial intelligence — "AI is one of the 7 large technology waves I've seen in my 4-decade technology career", 180 customer artificial-intelligence engagements, artificial-intelligence-native product revenue growing 47% year over year, and a new product for tracking how brands appear inside ChatGPT and Gemini answers. Two drivers have been quietly dropped: the count of customers paying more than one million dollars a year (retired as a disclosure — see section 5), and the goal of reaching the "Rule of 40" (a software benchmark where growth plus profit margin sums to 40), which Read spoke about in September 2025 and has not mentioned since.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management's claim | Where | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our best renewal rates since fiscal year '24" / "highest renewal rate in more than 2 years" | Q1 FY27 call | Net dollar expansion — how much more existing customers spend each year — went 102% (Q1 FY26) → 103% (Q4 FY26) → 104% (Q1 FY27). True, but the improvement is two percentage points over four quarters. | True, but trivially small |
| "Demand remains healthy... pipeline remains solid" | Every call since Dec 2025 | Quarterly revenue for the last four reported quarters: $219.1M, $220.6M, $219.5M, and guided $214–215M. Revenue has stopped growing and the current quarter is guided *down* sequentially. Full-year fiscal 2027 revenue is guided to $866.5–868.5M, about 1% growth. | Diverges — the story is richer than the numbers |
| "Strong adoption of our AI products" and 47% growth in artificial-intelligence product revenue | Q1 FY27 call | The growth is real but decelerating (50% for fiscal 2026, 47% in Q1 fiscal 2027), and management concedes it carries "higher cloud and data costs". | True, but see the gross-profit finding below |
| Improving profitability, "commitment to operating efficiency" | Q4 FY26 call | Fiscal 2026 operating profit before certain charges was $146.2M, up 63%. But the fiscal 2027 guide, issued 11 March 2026 at $144–146M, was **cut on 3 June 2026 to $139–141M**. Fiscal 2027 is a down year on operating profit. | Diverges — the trend reversed within one quarter |
| Earnings-per-share guidance was *raised* (from $0.47–0.48 to $0.48–0.49) | Q1 FY27 call | The operating-profit guide was cut by $5M at the same time. The per-share figure rose only because the assumed share count fell from 244M to 242M (buybacks) and assumed interest income rose from $15M to $20M. | **The per-share "raise" is financial engineering, not operations** |
| "Record $81 million in free cash flow" (Q1 FY26); "$65.8 million in free cash flow... a 30% free cash flow margin" (Q1 FY27) | Q1 calls | Both first quarters are the company's big collections quarter: receivables fell $81.2M in Q1 fiscal 2026 and $73.2M in Q1 fiscal 2027. Management guides only about **$10M of free cash flow in the current quarter**. The honest full-year number is the $150M guide, a 17% margin. | True but seasonal — the 30% margin is not repeatable |

### The single most important number in the file

In the quarter ended 30 April 2026, revenue grew 6.8% year over year, from $205.5M to $219.5M. Gross profit — revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the service — went from $142.869M to $143.031M. **That is growth of 0.1%. Fourteen million dollars of extra revenue produced one hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars of extra gross profit.**

Gross margin on a reported basis fell from 69.5% to 65.2%, a drop of 4.3 percentage points. On the company's own adjusted basis, subscription gross margin fell from 76% to 74% and total gross margin from 67% to 66%. The professional-services arm, which is 11% of revenue, is guided to a **negative 10% gross margin** this quarter — Sprinklr will pay for the privilege of delivering it.

Management's explanation is honest and consistent across four calls: "higher data and hosting costs in response to business opportunities, especially in Sprinklr Service and our expanded AI capabilities." That is the point. The artificial-intelligence products that carry the growth story are structurally less profitable than the social-listening business they are replacing. The chief financial officer called it "a structural shift for the long term" on the June 2026 call, then argued the current quarter is the bottom. That claim is testable in early September.

### One correction the screener's numbers require

The screener shows earnings per share down 79.8% year over year and return on invested capital of negative 3.4%. Both are accounting artefacts. In the quarter ended January 2025, Sprinklr recorded an **$83.3M tax benefit** (releasing a valuation allowance against deferred tax assets) on $15.4M of pre-tax income, producing $98.7M of quarterly net income and flattering fiscal 2025 to $122M. Fiscal 2026's $23M is the un-flattered figure. So the apparent earnings collapse did not happen. The flip side is equally important: **Sprinklr's genuine reported earnings power is about $23–29M a year on $871M of revenue** — a reported price-to-earnings ratio above 50 times. The company is far more profitable on its adjusted numbers than on its audited ones, and the gap is almost entirely share-based pay of roughly $80M a year.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a distinct softening in specificity.**

- *March 2025:* offensive and specific. "Fourth quarter the activity was stronger than expected... it was a bit better than expected." Names a 15% workforce reduction, names the customers (Delta, Ford, Ralph Lauren), names the metric (149 customers above one million dollars, up 18%).
- *June 2025:* first defensive turn. "The broader macroeconomic uncertainty has resulted in longer sales cycles and increased scrutiny of enterprise spending... resulting in more down-sell activity and, in some cases, logo churn." Customers above one million dollars now 146, growth cut from 18% to 6%.
- *September 2025:* defensive, with a leadership rupture (the chief financial officer's departure announced in the release). Read on margins: "we can stretch out the bottom line anytime we want" — a striking admission that the profit line is a dial, not an outcome.
- *December 2025:* the vocabulary turns abstract — "first-party data", "hyper-personalisation", "an operating system for modern customer experience". Fewer numbers, more category.
- *March 2026:* confident on process, hedged on timing. "We could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way."
- *June 2026:* the most emotionally invested call of the six. "Sorry, I got a little fired up there, Pat." Also the most careful: "I'm from Missouri, so I want to see it."

The pattern is a chief executive whose confidence in the *plan* is unwavering while his willingness to be pinned to a *date* has steadily declined. The language has moved from offence (growth, wins) to a hybrid of efficiency talk and category vision — the classic profile of a turnaround in its middle innings.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High for the next quarter. Low for the next year.**

This is the sharpest distinction in the file, and it matters for how you underwrite the stock.

*The quarter.* On 11 March 2026 the company guided the April quarter to $215.5–216.5M of revenue, $28.5–29.5M of adjusted operating profit and about $0.09 per share. It delivered $219.5M, $31.7M and $0.11. A clean beat on all three, consistent with the screener's record of beating in seven of the last seven quarters. On the March 2026 call the chief financial officer said plainly, "We delivered P&L guidance for the full year." There is a mild sandbagging pattern — the guide is set where it can be cleared — but there is no evidence of a missed quarter.

*The year.* The multi-year milestones have slipped roughly twelve months (section 1). And within fiscal 2027, the full-year operating-profit guide was cut from $144–146M to $139–141M just twelve weeks after it was issued, with the professional-services revenue assumption cut from $91M to $87M in the same breath. When an analyst from William Blair asked directly what had changed, the answer combined artificial-intelligence hosting costs, the services mix and the ViralMoment acquisition — three explanations for one cut.

The honest read: Sprinklr's management tells you accurately what will happen in ninety days and optimistically what will happen in three years.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The retired metric.** This is the most serious governance item in the file. The count of customers contributing at least one million dollars of annual subscription revenue went 149 (January 2025) → 146 (April 2025) → 145 (October 2025) → **141 (January 2026)**. On 11 March 2026, immediately after reporting the second consecutive sequential decline, the chief financial officer said: "We don't intend to disclose this metric quarterly going forward." On 3 June 2026 he confirmed the retirement.

Analysts pushed twice, hard, and got no direct answer either time.

- Jackson Ader (KeyBanc): "I'm surprised that the $1 million customer count and kind of cohort is not a part of sales incentives... because I think Project Bear Hug should be about maintaining and growing the largest customer cohort, and it seems like the disclosures are going the other way. So what am I missing?"
- Raimo Lenschow (Barclays): "are you taking that away because some customers on renewals are dropping below that?"

Neither question was answered. Read redirected to Bear Hug and to net dollar expansion; the chief financial officer redirected to "quality" and "share of wallet". **Retiring a declining disclosure, while declining to explain why, under direct and repeated challenge, is the classic tell.** It does not prove the number is getting worse — but it removes the investor's ability to check.

**The remaining-performance-obligation question.** Management now points investors to total contracted backlog, which crossed $1.04 billion in the April quarter, up 10% year over year. But current backlog (the part due within twelve months) grew only 5%, and revenue grew 1%. Management itself supplies the reason: "the majority of our renewal dollars are multiyear deals, which is driving an increase in the average contract length." Longer contracts mechanically inflate total backlog without adding a dollar of near-term revenue. Matthew VanVliet of Cantor asked about repeatability; Read's answer was that "5 to 7" deals of $3–10M and "3 to 5 customers" could be the next such deal, at a conversion rate he put at "even 50% or 45% or 40%".

**Red flags**

- **A genuinely pristine balance sheet.** $442.8M of cash and marketable securities against no borrowings at all (only $43.8M of lease obligations), giving about $399M of net cash — roughly 27% of the company's market value. Read: "I love the balance sheet, right, pristine."

- **Renewal and retention metrics are genuinely, if slowly, improving:** net dollar expansion 102% → 104% over four quarters, best renewal rate in more than two years, and 115% expansion inside the largest customer cohort.

## 7. Hidden signals

**A telling change of measuring stick.** In September 2025 Read framed the destination as "the March of the Rule of 40 — it has to have a combined growth component... You can't get there all on the bottom line." Fiscal 2027 is guided to roughly 1% growth and a 16% adjusted operating margin — a combined 17. The Rule of 40 has disappeared from the vocabulary, replaced by backlog, net dollar expansion and the count of artificial-intelligence engagements.

**The strategic-sale subtext, raised by an analyst and not disowned.** In June 2025 Patrick Walravens asked Read to walk through how his previous turnaround at Vonage ended in an Ericsson acquisition, and to "help us think about sort of what the strategic value of Sprinklr might be." Read answered by describing the phase framework rather than by declining the premise. There is no announced strategic process, no activist filing and no reported approach in any dated source through 27 July 2026 — this is inference, not evidence, and should be treated as such. But the chief executive's own track record is a real part of why some holders own the stock.

**Capital allocation language has hardened in the right direction.** In September 2025 Read declined to re-up the buyback, preferring to hold cash for "tuck-ins". By March 2026 the board authorised $200M and he said "we see the current share price as a compelling opportunity." By June 2026: "if there's an opportunity where we continue to see the stock lagging what we think its ultimate value is, we'll continue to leverage some of those dollars." That is the correct instinct from a management team that believes its own shares are cheap, and they have backed it with $125M in a single quarter.

**A new voice sounds different.** Anthony Coletta, chief financial officer since December 2025, introduced himself with a guidance philosophy — "we say what we do and we do what we mean... consistency and transparency." His first two guides have been the cut of March-to-June 2026 and the retirement of the customer-count metric. The stated philosophy and the first actions do not yet match.

**Concentration risk that nobody flagged.** Read disclosed the geographic mix as roughly 50–55% Americas, 35%-plus Europe, about 10% Asia, and separately described the Middle East as a meaningful region. In the April quarter, war damage forced the emergency migration of 54 customers off a Middle Eastern cloud facility to Ireland, and $3–4M of deals slipped. Management folded that into guidance, which is the right response — but it is a live, unhedged geopolitical exposure inside a business already guided to only 1% growth.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a deteriorating business and it is not yet a strengthening one. Renewals, retention, backlog and contract duration are all genuinely improving from a bad base; revenue and gross profit have gone flat; profitability is going backwards this year. A real transformation is under way and it is running about a year behind the schedule its architect originally implied.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, not the balance sheet, not the turnaround — the **gross-profit line**. Sprinklr's entire investment case rests on an assumption that the artificial-intelligence products it is winning on are worth having. In the April 2026 quarter they were not: 6.8% revenue growth converted into 0.1% gross-profit growth, because the cloud and data costs of serving artificial-intelligence workloads consumed the whole increment. If gross margin stabilises where management says it will and gross profit resumes growing, this is a cheap, cash-generative, net-cash franchise and the discount is a mispricing. If gross profit stays flat while revenue grows, then Sprinklr is buying revenue at zero marginal profit and every valuation multiple in the file is measuring a number that is not going to grow. The September and December 2026 reports settle it.

**Economic moat: switching costs, and eroding.**

The moat type is real and identifiable — switching costs from deep, multi-year enterprise implementations (the flagship deal spans 42 divisions and nearly 3,000 users; a contact-centre customer runs 5,000 agents across 210 countries), reinforced by an intangible data asset (more than 180 billion customer conversations a year, over a decade of language and intent modelling). Customers do not casually leave.

But the evidence says the moat is narrowing, not widening, and the test is the one the returns and margins impose:

- Gross margin is **falling** — 69.5% to 65.2% year over year on a reported basis, subscription margin 76% to 74% on the adjusted basis. A widening moat expands margin; this one is contracting.
- Net dollar expansion of 104% means the average existing customer spends four percent more each year. A wide switching-cost moat with real pricing power reads 110–120% or better. Sprinklr's own largest cohort manages 115% — the franchise is strong at the top and weak everywhere else, which is why the overall figure sits at 104%.
- The count of customers spending more than one million dollars a year **declined** for two consecutive quarters before disclosure was withdrawn.
- Returns on invested capital are, on audited numbers, close to zero.
- Management's own words: "renewal pressure that's been going on for two years" (June 2025); "we saw elevated churn in FY '26" (March 2026).

That combination — high but falling margin, sub-105% retention, a shrinking large-customer count — is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is the displacement of general-purpose software by generative artificial intelligence. It reaches Sprinklr from two directions. First on price and product: social listening, survey analytics and voice-of-the-customer work are exactly the categories where a large language model can produce "good enough" output cheaply, which caps what Sprinklr can charge. Second, and already visible in the accounts, on cost: the artificial-intelligence products Sprinklr sells to stay relevant carry materially worse unit economics than the products they replace — that is precisely why 6.8% revenue growth produced no gross profit.

It is material rather than terminal because Sprinklr also has genuine defences. Enterprise-grade data residency, security and compliance are not trivially replicated (the emergency migration of 54 customers from a damaged Middle Eastern facility to Ireland is the kind of thing that keeps a vendor in place). The contact-centre business is an operational deployment, not a content tool. Third parties still rank the platform a leader in two categories as of July 2026. And artificial-intelligence product revenue is growing 47%, which means Sprinklr is participating in the wave rather than only being hit by it.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap in the balance-sheet sense — there is no debt, $399M of net cash, $150M of guided free cash flow, and a buyback shrinking the share count 14% in two years. But it is not a clean fear-print either, because the low multiple sits on a gross-profit base that has stopped growing. Size it as what it is: a cheap, well-capitalised, mid-transformation franchise whose durability is genuinely unproven, and whose next two reports contain the number that decides which category it belongs to.

## 1. Narrative arc

This is a single, unbroken chief-executive narrative — and that is both its strength and the thing to be most careful about.

Rory Read took over as chief executive in late 2024 and, from his first call (March 2025), told investors exactly one story: a three-phase turnaround. Phase one is business optimisation (cut costs, redraw the sales territories, install a management reporting system). Phase two is transition and execution (embed the changes, fix the customer relationships). Phase three is acceleration (grow again). He has never deviated from that frame, he has never contradicted it, and he repeats the same vocabulary — "ambidextrous strategy", "business management system", "Project Bear Hug", "technical debt", "a work in progress" — in every call. Consistency of story is genuinely rare and it counts in his favour.

What has changed is the **clock**. In March 2025 the plan was: transition through fiscal 2026, "see the business begin to bend" during that year. By June 2025 he was saying "you look for a bend as we go through the second half into FY 2027". By March 2026 the acceleration phase had moved to fiscal 2028, and Patrick Walravens of Citizens JMP said so out loud: "previously, we thought the acceleration phase would happen in the second half of fiscal '27 and now we're talking about fiscal '28. Is that fair?" Read's answer did not deny it — he re-described the original ranges as "12 to 18 months" and added, "we could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way." By June 2026 the destination is unchanged and still one year out. **The story has not changed; the finish line has moved roughly twelve months in eighteen months of elapsed time.**

The content of the story has also shifted in one important way. In 2025 the growth driver was operational: fix renewals, fix implementations, sell to the Global 2000. By the March 2026 and June 2026 calls the growth driver is artificial intelligence — "AI is one of the 7 large technology waves I've seen in my 4-decade technology career", 180 customer artificial-intelligence engagements, artificial-intelligence-native product revenue growing 47% year over year, and a new product for tracking how brands appear inside ChatGPT and Gemini answers. ---

- **The disclosure retirement,** announced 11 March 2026 immediately after two consecutive declines in the metric, unexplained under two direct challenges (June 2026).

**A telling change of measuring stick.** In September 2025 Read framed the destination as "the March of the Rule of 40 — it has to have a combined growth component... **Capital allocation language has hardened in the right direction.** In September 2025 Read declined to re-up the buyback, preferring to hold cash for "tuck-ins". ## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a deteriorating business and it is not yet a strengthening one. Renewals, retention, backlog and contract duration are all genuinely improving from a bad base; revenue and gross profit have gone flat; profitability is going backwards this year. A real transformation is under way and it is running about a year behind the schedule its architect originally implied.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, not the balance sheet, not the turnaround — the **gross-profit line**. Sprinklr's entire investment case rests on an assumption that the artificial-intelligence products it is winning on are worth having. In the April 2026 quarter they were not: 6.8% revenue growth converted into 0.1% gross-profit growth, because the cloud and data costs of serving artificial-intelligence workloads consumed the whole increment. If gross margin stabilises where management says it will and gross profit resumes growing, this is a cheap, cash-generative, net-cash franchise and the discount is a mispricing. If gross profit stays flat while revenue grows, then Sprinklr is buying revenue at zero marginal profit and every valuation multiple in the file is measuring a number that is not going to grow. The September and December 2026 reports settle it.

**Economic moat: switching costs, and eroding.**

The moat type is real and identifiable — switching costs from deep, multi-year enterprise implementations (the flagship deal spans 42 divisions and nearly 3,000 users; a contact-centre customer runs 5,000 agents across 210 countries), reinforced by an intangible data asset (more than 180 billion customer conversations a year, over a decade of language and intent modelling). Customers do not casually leave.

But the evidence says the moat is narrowing, not widening, and the test is the one the returns and margins impose:

- Gross margin is **falling** — 69.5% to 65.2% year over year on a reported basis, subscription margin 76% to 74% on the adjusted basis. A widening moat expands margin; this one is contracting.
- Net dollar expansion of 104% means the average existing customer spends four percent more each year. A wide switching-cost moat with real pricing power reads 110–120% or better. Sprinklr's own largest cohort manages 115% — the franchise is strong at the top and weak everywhere else, which is why the overall figure sits at 104%.
- The count of customers spending more than one million dollars a year **declined** for two consecutive quarters before disclosure was withdrawn.
- Returns on invested capital are, on audited numbers, close to zero.
- Management's own words: "renewal pressure that's been going on for two years" (June 2025); "we saw elevated churn in FY '26" (March 2026).

That combination — high but falling margin, sub-105% retention, a shrinking large-customer count — is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is the displacement of general-purpose software by generative artificial intelligence. It reaches Sprinklr from two directions. First on price and product: social listening, survey analytics and voice-of-the-customer work are exactly the categories where a large language model can produce "good enough" output cheaply, which caps what Sprinklr can charge. Second, and already visible in the accounts, on cost: the artificial-intelligence products Sprinklr sells to stay relevant carry materially worse unit economics than the products they replace — that is precisely why 6.8% revenue growth produced no gross profit.

It is material rather than terminal because Sprinklr also has genuine defences. Enterprise-grade data residency, security and compliance are not trivially replicated (the emergency migration of 54 customers from a damaged Middle Eastern facility to Ireland is the kind of thing that keeps a vendor in place). The contact-centre business is an operational deployment, not a content tool. Third parties still rank the platform a leader in two categories as of July 2026. And artificial-intelligence product revenue is growing 47%, which means Sprinklr is participating in the wave rather than only being hit by it.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap in the balance-sheet sense — there is no debt, $399M of net cash, $150M of guided free cash flow, and a buyback shrinking the share count 14% in two years. But it is not a clean fear-print either, because the low multiple sits on a gross-profit base that has stopped growing. Size it as what it is: a cheap, well-capitalised, mid-transformation franchise whose durability is genuinely unproven, and whose next two reports contain the number that decides which category it belongs to.

interrogator_dossier:
# Sprinklr, Inc. (CXM) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $6.07 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars, intraday Monday 2026-07-27; up 6.9% from Friday's $5.685 close). Market value about $1.50 billion. The stock has traded between $4.72 and $9.40 over the past year, is down about 22% so far in 2026 and down about 35% over twelve months, but is up roughly 18% in the past month.

**Transcripts reviewed:** six consecutive quarterly calls — 2025-03-12 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2025), 2025-06-04, 2025-09-03, 2025-12-03, 2026-03-11 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2026) and 2026-06-03 (first quarter of fiscal 2027, retrieved live because it was missing from the supplied file). Sprinklr's fiscal year ends 31 January, so "fiscal 2027" is the year running to 31 January 2027.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

This is a single, unbroken chief-executive narrative — and that is both its strength and the thing to be most careful about.

Rory Read took over as chief executive in late 2024 and, from his first call (March 2025), told investors exactly one story: a three-phase turnaround. Phase one is business optimisation (cut costs, redraw the sales territories, install a management reporting system). Phase two is transition and execution (embed the changes, fix the customer relationships). Phase three is acceleration (grow again). He has never deviated from that frame, he has never contradicted it, and he repeats the same vocabulary — "ambidextrous strategy", "business management system", "Project Bear Hug", "technical debt", "a work in progress" — in every call. Consistency of story is genuinely rare and it counts in his favour.

What has changed is the **clock**. In March 2025 the plan was: transition through fiscal 2026, "see the business begin to bend" during that year. By June 2025 he was saying "you look for a bend as we go through the second half into FY 2027". By March 2026 the acceleration phase had moved to fiscal 2028, and Patrick Walravens of Citizens JMP said so out loud: "previously, we thought the acceleration phase would happen in the second half of fiscal '27 and now we're talking about fiscal '28. Is that fair?" Read's answer did not deny it — he re-described the original ranges as "12 to 18 months" and added, "we could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way." By June 2026 the destination is unchanged and still one year out. **The story has not changed; the finish line has moved roughly twelve months in eighteen months of elapsed time.**

The content of the story has also shifted in one important way. In 2025 the growth driver was operational: fix renewals, fix implementations, sell to the Global 2000. By the March 2026 and June 2026 calls the growth driver is artificial intelligence — "AI is one of the 7 large technology waves I've seen in my 4-decade technology career", 180 customer artificial-intelligence engagements, artificial-intelligence-native product revenue growing 47% year over year, and a new product for tracking how brands appear inside ChatGPT and Gemini answers. Two drivers have been quietly dropped: the count of customers paying more than one million dollars a year (retired as a disclosure — see section 5), and the goal of reaching the "Rule of 40" (a software benchmark where growth plus profit margin sums to 40), which Read spoke about in September 2025 and has not mentioned since.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management's claim | Where | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our best renewal rates since fiscal year '24" / "highest renewal rate in more than 2 years" | Q1 FY27 call | Net dollar expansion — how much more existing customers spend each year — went 102% (Q1 FY26) → 103% (Q4 FY26) → 104% (Q1 FY27). True, but the improvement is two percentage points over four quarters. | True, but trivially small |
| "Demand remains healthy... pipeline remains solid" | Every call since Dec 2025 | Quarterly revenue for the last four reported quarters: $219.1M, $220.6M, $219.5M, and guided $214–215M. Revenue has stopped growing and the current quarter is guided *down* sequentially. Full-year fiscal 2027 revenue is guided to $866.5–868.5M, about 1% growth. | Diverges — the story is richer than the numbers |
| "Strong adoption of our AI products" and 47% growth in artificial-intelligence product revenue | Q1 FY27 call | The growth is real but decelerating (50% for fiscal 2026, 47% in Q1 fiscal 2027), and management concedes it carries "higher cloud and data costs". | True, but see the gross-profit finding below |
| Improving profitability, "commitment to operating efficiency" | Q4 FY26 call | Fiscal 2026 operating profit before certain charges was $146.2M, up 63%. But the fiscal 2027 guide, issued 11 March 2026 at $144–146M, was **cut on 3 June 2026 to $139–141M**. Fiscal 2027 is a down year on operating profit. | Diverges — the trend reversed within one quarter |
| Earnings-per-share guidance was *raised* (from $0.47–0.48 to $0.48–0.49) | Q1 FY27 call | The operating-profit guide was cut by $5M at the same time. The per-share figure rose only because the assumed share count fell from 244M to 242M (buybacks) and assumed interest income rose from $15M to $20M. | **The per-share "raise" is financial engineering, not operations** |
| "Record $81 million in free cash flow" (Q1 FY26); "$65.8 million in free cash flow... a 30% free cash flow margin" (Q1 FY27) | Q1 calls | Both first quarters are the company's big collections quarter: receivables fell $81.2M in Q1 fiscal 2026 and $73.2M in Q1 fiscal 2027. Management guides only about **$10M of free cash flow in the current quarter**. The honest full-year number is the $150M guide, a 17% margin. | True but seasonal — the 30% margin is not repeatable |

### The single most important number in the file

In the quarter ended 30 April 2026, revenue grew 6.8% year over year, from $205.5M to $219.5M. Gross profit — revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the service — went from $142.869M to $143.031M. **That is growth of 0.1%. Fourteen million dollars of extra revenue produced one hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars of extra gross profit.**

Gross margin on a reported basis fell from 69.5% to 65.2%, a drop of 4.3 percentage points. On the company's own adjusted basis, subscription gross margin fell from 76% to 74% and total gross margin from 67% to 66%. The professional-services arm, which is 11% of revenue, is guided to a **negative 10% gross margin** this quarter — Sprinklr will pay for the privilege of delivering it.

Management's explanation is honest and consistent across four calls: "higher data and hosting costs in response to business opportunities, especially in Sprinklr Service and our expanded AI capabilities." That is the point. The artificial-intelligence products that carry the growth story are structurally less profitable than the social-listening business they are replacing. The chief financial officer called it "a structural shift for the long term" on the June 2026 call, then argued the current quarter is the bottom. That claim is testable in early September.

### One correction the screener's numbers require

The screener shows earnings per share down 79.8% year over year and return on invested capital of negative 3.4%. Both are accounting artefacts. In the quarter ended January 2025, Sprinklr recorded an **$83.3M tax benefit** (releasing a valuation allowance against deferred tax assets) on $15.4M of pre-tax income, producing $98.7M of quarterly net income and flattering fiscal 2025 to $122M. Fiscal 2026's $23M is the un-flattered figure. So the apparent earnings collapse did not happen. The flip side is equally important: **Sprinklr's genuine reported earnings power is about $23–29M a year on $871M of revenue** — a reported price-to-earnings ratio above 50 times. The company is far more profitable on its adjusted numbers than on its audited ones, and the gap is almost entirely share-based pay of roughly $80M a year.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a distinct softening in specificity.**

- *March 2025:* offensive and specific. "Fourth quarter the activity was stronger than expected... it was a bit better than expected." Names a 15% workforce reduction, names the customers (Delta, Ford, Ralph Lauren), names the metric (149 customers above one million dollars, up 18%).
- *June 2025:* first defensive turn. "The broader macroeconomic uncertainty has resulted in longer sales cycles and increased scrutiny of enterprise spending... resulting in more down-sell activity and, in some cases, logo churn." Customers above one million dollars now 146, growth cut from 18% to 6%.
- *September 2025:* defensive, with a leadership rupture (the chief financial officer's departure announced in the release). Read on margins: "we can stretch out the bottom line anytime we want" — a striking admission that the profit line is a dial, not an outcome.
- *December 2025:* the vocabulary turns abstract — "first-party data", "hyper-personalisation", "an operating system for modern customer experience". Fewer numbers, more category.
- *March 2026:* confident on process, hedged on timing. "We could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way."
- *June 2026:* the most emotionally invested call of the six. "Sorry, I got a little fired up there, Pat." Also the most careful: "I'm from Missouri, so I want to see it."

The pattern is a chief executive whose confidence in the *plan* is unwavering while his willingness to be pinned to a *date* has steadily declined. The language has moved from offence (growth, wins) to a hybrid of efficiency talk and category vision — the classic profile of a turnaround in its middle innings.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High for the next quarter. Low for the next year.**

This is the sharpest distinction in the file, and it matters for how you underwrite the stock.

*The quarter.* On 11 March 2026 the company guided the April quarter to $215.5–216.5M of revenue, $28.5–29.5M of adjusted operating profit and about $0.09 per share. It delivered $219.5M, $31.7M and $0.11. A clean beat on all three, consistent with the screener's record of beating in seven of the last seven quarters. On the March 2026 call the chief financial officer said plainly, "We delivered P&L guidance for the full year." There is a mild sandbagging pattern — the guide is set where it can be cleared — but there is no evidence of a missed quarter.

*The year.* The multi-year milestones have slipped roughly twelve months (section 1). And within fiscal 2027, the full-year operating-profit guide was cut from $144–146M to $139–141M just twelve weeks after it was issued, with the professional-services revenue assumption cut from $91M to $87M in the same breath. When an analyst from William Blair asked directly what had changed, the answer combined artificial-intelligence hosting costs, the services mix and the ViralMoment acquisition — three explanations for one cut.

The honest read: Sprinklr's management tells you accurately what will happen in ninety days and optimistically what will happen in three years.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The retired metric.** This is the most serious governance item in the file. The count of customers contributing at least one million dollars of annual subscription revenue went 149 (January 2025) → 146 (April 2025) → 145 (October 2025) → **141 (January 2026)**. On 11 March 2026, immediately after reporting the second consecutive sequential decline, the chief financial officer said: "We don't intend to disclose this metric quarterly going forward." On 3 June 2026 he confirmed the retirement.

Analysts pushed twice, hard, and got no direct answer either time.

- Jackson Ader (KeyBanc): "I'm surprised that the $1 million customer count and kind of cohort is not a part of sales incentives... because I think Project Bear Hug should be about maintaining and growing the largest customer cohort, and it seems like the disclosures are going the other way. So what am I missing?"
- Raimo Lenschow (Barclays): "are you taking that away because some customers on renewals are dropping below that?"

Neither question was answered. Read redirected to Bear Hug and to net dollar expansion; the chief financial officer redirected to "quality" and "share of wallet". **Retiring a declining disclosure, while declining to explain why, under direct and repeated challenge, is the classic tell.** It does not prove the number is getting worse — but it removes the investor's ability to check.

**The remaining-performance-obligation question.** Management now points investors to total contracted backlog, which crossed $1.04 billion in the April quarter, up 10% year over year. But current backlog (the part due within twelve months) grew only 5%, and revenue grew 1%. Management itself supplies the reason: "the majority of our renewal dollars are multiyear deals, which is driving an increase in the average contract length." Longer contracts mechanically inflate total backlog without adding a dollar of near-term revenue. Backlog is being offered as the growth proof precisely as revenue stops growing, and the single largest software deal in company history — one contract, one global consumer-electronics customer, 42 divisions — is what pushed it past the billion-dollar mark. Matthew VanVliet of Cantor asked about repeatability; Read's answer was that "5 to 7" deals of $3–10M and "3 to 5 customers" could be the next such deal, at a conversion rate he put at "even 50% or 45% or 40%".

**What analysts have not pressed hard enough on.** Nobody has asked why revenue growth produced no incremental gross profit. Morgan Stanley's associate came closest ("should we be viewing this quarter's gross margin level... as kind of the trough?") and received an assurance rather than a bridge.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Gross profit dollars are flat.** Up 0.1% year over year in the April 2026 quarter on 6.8% revenue growth. The growth engine is not creating profit.
- **The disclosure retirement,** announced 11 March 2026 immediately after two consecutive declines in the metric, unexplained under two direct challenges (June 2026).

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a deteriorating business and it is not yet a strengthening one. Renewals, retention, backlog and contract duration are all genuinely improving from a bad base; revenue and gross profit have gone flat; profitability is going backwards this year. A real transformation is under way and it is running about a year behind the schedule its architect originally implied.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, not the balance sheet, not the turnaround — the **gross-profit line**. Sprinklr's entire investment case rests on an assumption that the artificial-intelligence products it is winning on are worth having. In the April 2026 quarter they were not: 6.8% revenue growth converted into 0.1% gross-profit growth, because the cloud and data costs of serving artificial-intelligence workloads consumed the whole increment. If gross margin stabilises where management says it will and gross profit resumes growing, this is a cheap, cash-generative, net-cash franchise and the discount is a mispricing. If gross profit stays flat while revenue grows, then Sprinklr is buying revenue at zero marginal profit and every valuation multiple in the file is measuring a number that is not going to grow. The September and December 2026 reports settle it.

**Economic moat: switching costs, and eroding.**

The moat type is real and identifiable — switching costs from deep, multi-year enterprise implementations (the flagship deal spans 42 divisions and nearly 3,000 users; a contact-centre customer runs 5,000 agents across 210 countries), reinforced by an intangible data asset (more than 180 billion customer conversations a year, over a decade of language and intent modelling). Customers do not casually leave.

But the evidence says the moat is narrowing, not widening, and the test is the one the returns and margins impose:

- Gross margin is **falling** — 69.5% to 65.2% year over year on a reported basis, subscription margin 76% to 74% on the adjusted basis. A widening moat expands margin; this one is contracting.
- Net dollar expansion of 104% means the average existing customer spends four percent more each year. A wide switching-cost moat with real pricing power reads 110–120% or better. Sprinklr's own largest cohort manages 115% — the franchise is strong at the top and weak everywhere else, which is why the overall figure sits at 104%.
- The count of customers spending more than one million dollars a year **declined** for two consecutive quarters before disclosure was withdrawn.
- Returns on invested capital are, on audited numbers, close to zero.
- Management's own words: "renewal pressure that's been going on for two years" (June 2025); "we saw elevated churn in FY '26" (March 2026).

That combination — high but falling margin, sub-105% retention, a shrinking large-customer count — is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is the displacement of general-purpose software by generative artificial intelligence. It reaches Sprinklr from two directions. First on price and product: social listening, survey analytics and voice-of-the-customer work are exactly the categories where a large language model can produce "good enough" output cheaply, which caps what Sprinklr can charge. Second, and already visible in the accounts, on cost: the artificial-intelligence products Sprinklr sells to stay relevant carry materially worse unit economics than the products they replace — that is precisely why 6.8% revenue growth produced no gross profit.

It is material rather than terminal because Sprinklr also has genuine defences. Enterprise-grade data residency, security and compliance are not trivially replicated (the emergency migration of 54 customers from a damaged Middle Eastern facility to Ireland is the kind of thing that keeps a vendor in place). The contact-centre business is an operational deployment, not a content tool. Third parties still rank the platform a leader in two categories as of July 2026. And artificial-intelligence product revenue is growing 47%, which means Sprinklr is participating in the wave rather than only being hit by it.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap in the balance-sheet sense — there is no debt, $399M of net cash, $150M of guided free cash flow, and a buyback shrinking the share count 14% in two years. But it is not a clean fear-print either, because the low multiple sits on a gross-profit base that has stopped growing. Size it as what it is: a cheap, well-capitalised, mid-transformation franchise whose durability is genuinely unproven, and whose next two reports contain the number that decides which category it belongs to.

On the measure this screen uses, enterprise value to gross profit, Sprinklr sits near 1.9 times against roughly 4.3 times for Adobe, 3.9 for HubSpot and 5.3 for Salesforce - a discount of about 55% to the median. The discount is genuinely large but it is earned rather than mistaken: Adobe earns a 36% return on invested capital and Salesforce 9%, while Sprinklr's audited returns are close to zero; all three peers are still growing gross profit while Sprinklr's was flat at plus 0.1% last quarter. One further caution on how much of this is Sprinklr-specific. Adobe at 3.8 times revenue and 9.1 times free cash flow is itself a de-rated print, and it is de-rated on the same unresolved question that hangs over Sprinklr - whether generative artificial intelligence compresses the pricing power of seat-based software. A meaningful part of Sprinklr's discount is therefore shared sector pressure rather than a mispricing of this particular company, and should not be counted as edge specific to the name.

# Sprinklr, Inc. (CXM) — Forensic Dossier

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $6.07 (New York Stock Exchange, US dollars, intraday Monday 2026-07-27; up 6.9% from Friday's $5.685 close). Market value about $1.50 billion. The stock has traded between $4.72 and $9.40 over the past year, is down about 22% so far in 2026 and down about 35% over twelve months, but is up roughly 18% in the past month.

**Transcripts reviewed:** six consecutive quarterly calls — 2025-03-12 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2025), 2025-06-04, 2025-09-03, 2025-12-03, 2026-03-11 (fourth quarter of fiscal 2026) and 2026-06-03 (first quarter of fiscal 2027, retrieved live because it was missing from the supplied file). Sprinklr's fiscal year ends 31 January, so "fiscal 2027" is the year running to 31 January 2027.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

This is a single, unbroken chief-executive narrative — and that is both its strength and the thing to be most careful about.

Rory Read took over as chief executive in late 2024 and, from his first call (March 2025), told investors exactly one story: a three-phase turnaround. Phase one is business optimisation (cut costs, redraw the sales territories, install a management reporting system). Phase two is transition and execution (embed the changes, fix the customer relationships). Phase three is acceleration (grow again). He has never deviated from that frame, he has never contradicted it, and he repeats the same vocabulary — "ambidextrous strategy", "business management system", "Project Bear Hug", "technical debt", "a work in progress" — in every call. Consistency of story is genuinely rare and it counts in his favour.

What has changed is the **clock**. In March 2025 the plan was: transition through fiscal 2026, "see the business begin to bend" during that year. By June 2025 he was saying "you look for a bend as we go through the second half into FY 2027". By March 2026 the acceleration phase had moved to fiscal 2028, and Patrick Walravens of Citizens JMP said so out loud: "previously, we thought the acceleration phase would happen in the second half of fiscal '27 and now we're talking about fiscal '28. Is that fair?" Read's answer did not deny it — he re-described the original ranges as "12 to 18 months" and added, "we could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way." By June 2026 the destination is unchanged and still one year out. **The story has not changed; the finish line has moved roughly twelve months in eighteen months of elapsed time.**

The content of the story has also shifted in one important way. In 2025 the growth driver was operational: fix renewals, fix implementations, sell to the Global 2000. By the March 2026 and June 2026 calls the growth driver is artificial intelligence — "AI is one of the 7 large technology waves I've seen in my 4-decade technology career", 180 customer artificial-intelligence engagements, artificial-intelligence-native product revenue growing 47% year over year, and a new product for tracking how brands appear inside ChatGPT and Gemini answers. Two drivers have been quietly dropped: the count of customers paying more than one million dollars a year (retired as a disclosure — see section 5), and the goal of reaching the "Rule of 40" (a software benchmark where growth plus profit margin sums to 40), which Read spoke about in September 2025 and has not mentioned since.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

| Management's claim | Where | What the numbers actually show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Our best renewal rates since fiscal year '24" / "highest renewal rate in more than 2 years" | Q1 FY27 call | Net dollar expansion — how much more existing customers spend each year — went 102% (Q1 FY26) → 103% (Q4 FY26) → 104% (Q1 FY27). True, but the improvement is two percentage points over four quarters. | True, but trivially small |
| "Demand remains healthy... pipeline remains solid" | Every call since Dec 2025 | Quarterly revenue for the last four reported quarters: $219.1M, $220.6M, $219.5M, and guided $214–215M. Revenue has stopped growing and the current quarter is guided *down* sequentially. Full-year fiscal 2027 revenue is guided to $866.5–868.5M, about 1% growth. | Diverges — the story is richer than the numbers |
| "Strong adoption of our AI products" and 47% growth in artificial-intelligence product revenue | Q1 FY27 call | The growth is real but decelerating (50% for fiscal 2026, 47% in Q1 fiscal 2027), and management concedes it carries "higher cloud and data costs". | True, but see the gross-profit finding below |
| Improving profitability, "commitment to operating efficiency" | Q4 FY26 call | Fiscal 2026 operating profit before certain charges was $146.2M, up 63%. But the fiscal 2027 guide, issued 11 March 2026 at $144–146M, was **cut on 3 June 2026 to $139–141M**. Fiscal 2027 is a down year on operating profit. | Diverges — the trend reversed within one quarter |
| Earnings-per-share guidance was *raised* (from $0.47–0.48 to $0.48–0.49) | Q1 FY27 call | The operating-profit guide was cut by $5M at the same time. The per-share figure rose only because the assumed share count fell from 244M to 242M (buybacks) and assumed interest income rose from $15M to $20M. | **The per-share "raise" is financial engineering, not operations** |
| "Record $81 million in free cash flow" (Q1 FY26); "$65.8 million in free cash flow... a 30% free cash flow margin" (Q1 FY27) | Q1 calls | Both first quarters are the company's big collections quarter: receivables fell $81.2M in Q1 fiscal 2026 and $73.2M in Q1 fiscal 2027. Management guides only about **$10M of free cash flow in the current quarter**. The honest full-year number is the $150M guide, a 17% margin. | True but seasonal — the 30% margin is not repeatable |

### The single most important number in the file

In the quarter ended 30 April 2026, revenue grew 6.8% year over year, from $205.5M to $219.5M. Gross profit — revenue minus the direct cost of delivering the service — went from $142.869M to $143.031M. **That is growth of 0.1%. Fourteen million dollars of extra revenue produced one hundred and sixty-two thousand dollars of extra gross profit.**

Gross margin on a reported basis fell from 69.5% to 65.2%, a drop of 4.3 percentage points. On the company's own adjusted basis, subscription gross margin fell from 76% to 74% and total gross margin from 67% to 66%. The professional-services arm, which is 11% of revenue, is guided to a **negative 10% gross margin** this quarter — Sprinklr will pay for the privilege of delivering it.

Management's explanation is honest and consistent across four calls: "higher data and hosting costs in response to business opportunities, especially in Sprinklr Service and our expanded AI capabilities." That is the point. The artificial-intelligence products that carry the growth story are structurally less profitable than the social-listening business they are replacing. The chief financial officer called it "a structural shift for the long term" on the June 2026 call, then argued the current quarter is the bottom. That claim is testable in early September.

### One correction the screener's numbers require

The screener shows earnings per share down 79.8% year over year and return on invested capital of negative 3.4%. Both are accounting artefacts. In the quarter ended January 2025, Sprinklr recorded an **$83.3M tax benefit** (releasing a valuation allowance against deferred tax assets) on $15.4M of pre-tax income, producing $98.7M of quarterly net income and flattering fiscal 2025 to $122M. Fiscal 2026's $23M is the un-flattered figure. So the apparent earnings collapse did not happen. The flip side is equally important: **Sprinklr's genuine reported earnings power is about $23–29M a year on $871M of revenue** — a reported price-to-earnings ratio above 50 times. The company is far more profitable on its adjusted numbers than on its audited ones, and the gap is almost entirely share-based pay of roughly $80M a year.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: Stable, with a distinct softening in specificity.**

- *March 2025:* offensive and specific. "Fourth quarter the activity was stronger than expected... it was a bit better than expected." Names a 15% workforce reduction, names the customers (Delta, Ford, Ralph Lauren), names the metric (149 customers above one million dollars, up 18%).
- *June 2025:* first defensive turn. "The broader macroeconomic uncertainty has resulted in longer sales cycles and increased scrutiny of enterprise spending... resulting in more down-sell activity and, in some cases, logo churn." Customers above one million dollars now 146, growth cut from 18% to 6%.
- *September 2025:* defensive, with a leadership rupture (the chief financial officer's departure announced in the release). Read on margins: "we can stretch out the bottom line anytime we want" — a striking admission that the profit line is a dial, not an outcome.
- *December 2025:* the vocabulary turns abstract — "first-party data", "hyper-personalisation", "an operating system for modern customer experience". Fewer numbers, more category.
- *March 2026:* confident on process, hedged on timing. "We could be 3, 6 months, give or take, either way."
- *June 2026:* the most emotionally invested call of the six. "Sorry, I got a little fired up there, Pat." Also the most careful: "I'm from Missouri, so I want to see it."

The pattern is a chief executive whose confidence in the *plan* is unwavering while his willingness to be pinned to a *date* has steadily declined. The language has moved from offence (growth, wins) to a hybrid of efficiency talk and category vision — the classic profile of a turnaround in its middle innings.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability: High for the next quarter. Low for the next year.**

This is the sharpest distinction in the file, and it matters for how you underwrite the stock.

*The quarter.* On 11 March 2026 the company guided the April quarter to $215.5–216.5M of revenue, $28.5–29.5M of adjusted operating profit and about $0.09 per share. It delivered $219.5M, $31.7M and $0.11. A clean beat on all three, consistent with the screener's record of beating in seven of the last seven quarters. On the March 2026 call the chief financial officer said plainly, "We delivered P&L guidance for the full year." There is a mild sandbagging pattern — the guide is set where it can be cleared — but there is no evidence of a missed quarter.

*The year.* The multi-year milestones have slipped roughly twelve months (section 1). And within fiscal 2027, the full-year operating-profit guide was cut from $144–146M to $139–141M just twelve weeks after it was issued, with the professional-services revenue assumption cut from $91M to $87M in the same breath. When an analyst from William Blair asked directly what had changed, the answer combined artificial-intelligence hosting costs, the services mix and the ViralMoment acquisition — three explanations for one cut.

The honest read: Sprinklr's management tells you accurately what will happen in ninety days and optimistically what will happen in three years.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**The retired metric.** This is the most serious governance item in the file. The count of customers contributing at least one million dollars of annual subscription revenue went 149 (January 2025) → 146 (April 2025) → 145 (October 2025) → **141 (January 2026)**. On 11 March 2026, immediately after reporting the second consecutive sequential decline, the chief financial officer said: "We don't intend to disclose this metric quarterly going forward." On 3 June 2026 he confirmed the retirement.

Analysts pushed twice, hard, and got no direct answer either time.

- Jackson Ader (KeyBanc): "I'm surprised that the $1 million customer count and kind of cohort is not a part of sales incentives... because I think Project Bear Hug should be about maintaining and growing the largest customer cohort, and it seems like the disclosures are going the other way. So what am I missing?"
- Raimo Lenschow (Barclays): "are you taking that away because some customers on renewals are dropping below that?"

Neither question was answered. Read redirected to Bear Hug and to net dollar expansion; the chief financial officer redirected to "quality" and "share of wallet". **Retiring a declining disclosure, while declining to explain why, under direct and repeated challenge, is the classic tell.** It does not prove the number is getting worse — but it removes the investor's ability to check.

**The remaining-performance-obligation question.** Management now points investors to total contracted backlog, which crossed $1.04 billion in the April quarter, up 10% year over year. But current backlog (the part due within twelve months) grew only 5%, and revenue grew 1%. Management itself supplies the reason: "the majority of our renewal dollars are multiyear deals, which is driving an increase in the average contract length." Longer contracts mechanically inflate total backlog without adding a dollar of near-term revenue. Backlog is being offered as the growth proof precisely as revenue stops growing, and the single largest software deal in company history — one contract, one global consumer-electronics customer, 42 divisions — is what pushed it past the billion-dollar mark. Matthew VanVliet of Cantor asked about repeatability; Read's answer was that "5 to 7" deals of $3–10M and "3 to 5 customers" could be the next such deal, at a conversion rate he put at "even 50% or 45% or 40%".

**What analysts have not pressed hard enough on.** Nobody has asked why revenue growth produced no incremental gross profit. Morgan Stanley's associate came closest ("should we be viewing this quarter's gross margin level... as kind of the trough?") and received an assurance rather than a bridge.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **Gross profit dollars are flat.** Up 0.1% year over year in the April 2026 quarter on 6.8% revenue growth. The growth engine is not creating profit.
- **The disclosure retirement,** announced 11 March 2026 immediately after two consecutive declines in the metric, unexplained under two direct challenges (June 2026).
- **Insider selling is one-sided.** On open-market transactions only: one purchase of twenty shares against fifty-eight sales totalling 11.3 million shares. The screener's headline insider ratio is inflated by option grants; the open-market record is the real signal.
- **Chief revenue officer turnover inside ten months.** Scott Millar was announced as chief revenue officer on 3 September 2025 and presented as a transformative hire ("led a $15 billion revenue organization"). On 1 July 2026, Thomas Addis was announced as chief revenue officer, effective immediately. In December 2025 Read had said the leadership team was "nearly complete."
- **A one-year slip in the acceleration date** (fiscal 2027 second half to fiscal 2028), conceded only under analyst prompting on 11 March 2026.
- **Professional-services gross margin guided to negative 10%** for the quarter ending July 2026 — a revenue line the company loses money on, at 11% of the total.
- **Operating-profit guidance cut** twelve weeks after issue, masked by a per-share figure that rose on buybacks and interest income.

**Green flags**

- **A genuinely pristine balance sheet.** $442.8M of cash and marketable securities against no borrowings at all (only $43.8M of lease obligations), giving about $399M of net cash — roughly 27% of the company's market value. Read: "I love the balance sheet, right, pristine."
- **Real, repeated capital return.** A $200M buyback authorised 11 March 2026, of which a $125M accelerated repurchase retired 17.1 million shares in a single quarter; $75M remained as of 29 May 2026, with the programme to complete by 15 March 2027. Diluted share count has fallen from 284.0 million (April 2024) to 243.1 million (April 2026), a 14% reduction — the buybacks are comfortably absorbing the share-based pay.
- **Free cash flow is real and rising.** $142M in fiscal 2026, up 140%, guided to $150M in fiscal 2027.
- **Ninety-day guidance is reliable** — seven consecutive quarters of beats, and the April quarter beat all three guided lines.
- **Renewal and retention metrics are genuinely, if slowly, improving:** net dollar expansion 102% → 104% over four quarters, best renewal rate in more than two years, and 115% expansion inside the largest customer cohort.
- **Independent third-party validation.** Named a Leader in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant for Voice of the Customer (13 March 2026) and for Social Media Management and Listening (8 July 2026, placed furthest on vision and highest on execution).

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**A telling change of measuring stick.** In September 2025 Read framed the destination as "the March of the Rule of 40 — it has to have a combined growth component... You can't get there all on the bottom line." Fiscal 2027 is guided to roughly 1% growth and a 16% adjusted operating margin — a combined 17. The Rule of 40 has disappeared from the vocabulary, replaced by backlog, net dollar expansion and the count of artificial-intelligence engagements.

**The strategic-sale subtext, raised by an analyst and not disowned.** In June 2025 Patrick Walravens asked Read to walk through how his previous turnaround at Vonage ended in an Ericsson acquisition, and to "help us think about sort of what the strategic value of Sprinklr might be." Read answered by describing the phase framework rather than by declining the premise. There is no announced strategic process, no activist filing and no reported approach in any dated source through 27 July 2026 — this is inference, not evidence, and should be treated as such. But the chief executive's own track record is a real part of why some holders own the stock.

**Capital allocation language has hardened in the right direction.** In September 2025 Read declined to re-up the buyback, preferring to hold cash for "tuck-ins". By March 2026 the board authorised $200M and he said "we see the current share price as a compelling opportunity." By June 2026: "if there's an opportunity where we continue to see the stock lagging what we think its ultimate value is, we'll continue to leverage some of those dollars." That is the correct instinct from a management team that believes its own shares are cheap, and they have backed it with $125M in a single quarter.

**A new voice sounds different.** Anthony Coletta, chief financial officer since December 2025, introduced himself with a guidance philosophy — "we say what we do and we do what we mean... consistency and transparency." His first two guides have been the cut of March-to-June 2026 and the retirement of the customer-count metric. The stated philosophy and the first actions do not yet match.

**Concentration risk that nobody flagged.** Read disclosed the geographic mix as roughly 50–55% Americas, 35%-plus Europe, about 10% Asia, and separately described the Middle East as a meaningful region. In the April quarter, war damage forced the emergency migration of 54 customers off a Middle Eastern cloud facility to Ireland, and $3–4M of deals slipped. Management folded that into guidance, which is the right response — but it is a live, unhedged geopolitical exposure inside a business already guided to only 1% growth.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING.** This is not a deteriorating business and it is not yet a strengthening one. Renewals, retention, backlog and contract duration are all genuinely improving from a bad base; revenue and gross profit have gone flat; profitability is going backwards this year. A real transformation is under way and it is running about a year behind the schedule its architect originally implied.

**The single thing to weigh before sizing.** Not the valuation, not the balance sheet, not the turnaround — the **gross-profit line**. Sprinklr's entire investment case rests on an assumption that the artificial-intelligence products it is winning on are worth having. In the April 2026 quarter they were not: 6.8% revenue growth converted into 0.1% gross-profit growth, because the cloud and data costs of serving artificial-intelligence workloads consumed the whole increment. If gross margin stabilises where management says it will and gross profit resumes growing, this is a cheap, cash-generative, net-cash franchise and the discount is a mispricing. If gross profit stays flat while revenue grows, then Sprinklr is buying revenue at zero marginal profit and every valuation multiple in the file is measuring a number that is not going to grow. The September and December 2026 reports settle it.

**Economic moat: switching costs, and eroding.**

The moat type is real and identifiable — switching costs from deep, multi-year enterprise implementations (the flagship deal spans 42 divisions and nearly 3,000 users; a contact-centre customer runs 5,000 agents across 210 countries), reinforced by an intangible data asset (more than 180 billion customer conversations a year, over a decade of language and intent modelling). Customers do not casually leave.

But the evidence says the moat is narrowing, not widening, and the test is the one the returns and margins impose:

- Gross margin is **falling** — 69.5% to 65.2% year over year on a reported basis, subscription margin 76% to 74% on the adjusted basis. A widening moat expands margin; this one is contracting.
- Net dollar expansion of 104% means the average existing customer spends four percent more each year. A wide switching-cost moat with real pricing power reads 110–120% or better. Sprinklr's own largest cohort manages 115% — the franchise is strong at the top and weak everywhere else, which is why the overall figure sits at 104%.
- The count of customers spending more than one million dollars a year **declined** for two consecutive quarters before disclosure was withdrawn.
- Returns on invested capital are, on audited numbers, close to zero.
- Management's own words: "renewal pressure that's been going on for two years" (June 2025); "we saw elevated churn in FY '26" (March 2026).

That combination — high but falling margin, sub-105% retention, a shrinking large-customer count — is an eroding moat, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: material, not terminal.** The structural force is the displacement of general-purpose software by generative artificial intelligence. It reaches Sprinklr from two directions. First on price and product: social listening, survey analytics and voice-of-the-customer work are exactly the categories where a large language model can produce "good enough" output cheaply, which caps what Sprinklr can charge. Second, and already visible in the accounts, on cost: the artificial-intelligence products Sprinklr sells to stay relevant carry materially worse unit economics than the products they replace — that is precisely why 6.8% revenue growth produced no gross profit.

It is material rather than terminal because Sprinklr also has genuine defences. Enterprise-grade data residency, security and compliance are not trivially replicated (the emergency migration of 54 customers from a damaged Middle Eastern facility to Ireland is the kind of thing that keeps a vendor in place). The contact-centre business is an operational deployment, not a content tool. Third parties still rank the platform a leader in two categories as of July 2026. And artificial-intelligence product revenue is growing 47%, which means Sprinklr is participating in the wave rather than only being hit by it.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a value trap?** Neither cleanly, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap in the balance-sheet sense — there is no debt, $399M of net cash, $150M of guided free cash flow, and a buyback shrinking the share count 14% in two years. But it is not a clean fear-print either, because the low multiple sits on a gross-profit base that has stopped growing. Size it as what it is: a cheap, well-capitalised, mid-transformation franchise whose durability is genuinely unproven, and whose next two reports contain the number that decides which category it belongs to.
